title: The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere

meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere, specification section 4.9.1.
final_note: You worked through The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere — 16 specification statements.

concepts.def: For the last 200 million years the proportions of the different gases in the atmosphere have been much the same as they are today. The atmosphere has therefore been broadly stable over that period, but was very different before it.
Nitrogen makes up about four-fifths (approximately 80%) of the atmosphere. It is the most abundant gas in the air today.
Oxygen makes up about one-fifth (approximately 20%) of the atmosphere. It is the second most abundant gas in the air today.

The remainder of the atmosphere is made up of small proportions of various other gases, including carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases. Together these account for only a small proportion of the air.

concepts.term: Why evidence for the early atmosphere is limited
concepts.def: Evidence for the Earth's early atmosphere is limited because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years. Scientists cannot sample an atmosphere that existed billions of years ago, so conclusions rest on indirect evidence.

Theories about what was in the Earth's early atmosphere and how the atmosphere was formed have changed and developed over time. A theory is the current best explanation of the available evidence and is revised as new evidence is found.
One theory suggests that during the first billion years of the Earth's existence there was intense volcanic activity that released the gases which formed the early atmosphere.
The same volcanic activity released water vapour, which condensed to form the oceans as the Earth cooled.
At the start of this period the Earth's atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today, consisting of mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.
Volcanoes also produced nitrogen, which gradually built up in the atmosphere. Because nitrogen is unreactive it was not readily removed, so its proportion increased over time.
There may also have been small proportions of methane and ammonia in the early atmosphere.
When the oceans formed, carbon dioxide dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated, producing sediments. This reduced the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

concepts.term: Evaluating theories about the early atmosphere
concepts.def: Given appropriate information, students should be able to interpret evidence and evaluate different theories about the Earth's early atmosphere, judging how far the evidence supports a claim and where its limitations lie.

Algae and plants produced the oxygen that is now in the atmosphere by photosynthesis, which can be represented by the equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, that is, carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.

Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago and soon after this oxygen appeared in the atmosphere. Over the next billion years plants evolved and the percentage of oxygen gradually increased to a level that enabled animals to evolve.
Algae and plants decreased the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere by photosynthesis, because the reaction uses carbon dioxide as a reactant.

concepts.term: Carbon locked into rocks and fuels
concepts.def: Carbon dioxide was also decreased by the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon. Carbon taken from the atmosphere by living organisms was buried and retained in these deposits.

Limestone is a sedimentary rock formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms, which are made of calcium carbonate. These deposits built up on the sea bed and were buried and compressed, locking carbon into the rock.

Coal is a sedimentary rock formed from thick deposits of plant material. The plants were buried by sediment and, over millions of years, heat and pressure in the absence of oxygen converted the deposits to coal.

concepts.term: Formation of crude oil and natural gas
concepts.def: Crude oil and natural gas were formed from the remains of plankton (marine organisms) that were buried in mud on the sea bed and changed over millions of years by heat and pressure in the absence of oxygen.

concepts.term: Main changes in the atmosphere over time
concepts.def: The main changes are a large decrease in carbon dioxide and an increase in oxygen. Carbon dioxide fell because it dissolved in the oceans and was precipitated as carbonates, was used in photosynthesis, and was locked into sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels; oxygen rose because algae and then plants photosynthesised.

mcqs.q: For roughly how long have the proportions of the different gases in the atmosphere been much the same as they are today?
options: About 4.6 billion years
About 2.7 billion years
About one billion years
About 200 million years
mcqs.explain: The specification states that for 200 million years the proportions of the different gases have been much the same as they are today.

mcqs.q: Which of these best describes the proportions of the two main gases in the atmosphere today?
options: About 80% oxygen and about 20% nitrogen
About 80% nitrogen, about 20% oxygen
About 80% nitrogen, 20% carbon dioxide
About 50% nitrogen and 50% oxygen gas
mcqs.explain: Nitrogen is about four-fifths (approximately 80%) of the atmosphere and oxygen about one-fifth (approximately 20%).

mcqs.q: Which statement about carbon dioxide, water vapour and the noble gases in the air today is correct?
options: Together they make up a small part.
Together they make up about one fifth.
Carbon dioxide alone makes up about 20%.
The noble gases make up about one fifth.
mcqs.explain: The specification describes these as small proportions of various other gases, left after about 80% nitrogen and about 20% oxygen.

mcqs.q: Why is the evidence about the Earth's early atmosphere limited?
options: Instruments to measure it have not been built.
The time scale involved is 4.6 billion years.
There is no evidence about it left at all.
The early atmosphere had undetectable gases.
mcqs.explain: The specification gives exactly this reason: evidence is limited because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years.

mcqs.q: Theories about the Earth's early atmosphere have changed and developed over time. What does this best show?
options: The earlier scientists were careless in their own research.
Evidence about the early atmosphere is now complete.
Scientific ideas about the distant past are never reliable.
Explanations are revised when new evidence appears.
mcqs.explain: Theories are the current best explanation of the available evidence and develop as more evidence is gathered.

mcqs.q: According to the theory in the specification, what was the Earth's atmosphere like at the start of its first billion years?
options: Oxygen, with little or no carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide, with little or no oxygen
Nitrogen, with little or no carbon dioxide
Methane, with a large amount of oxygen
mcqs.explain: The specification states the atmosphere may have been like those of Mars and Venus today, mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.

mcqs.q: Scientists use the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today as a model for the Earth's early atmosphere. Why?
options: They consist of nitrogen and oxygen.
They have the same atmosphere as us.
They consist mainly of carbon dioxide today.
They have no atmosphere at all to compare.
mcqs.explain: The specification says the early Earth's atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus, mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen.

mcqs.q: According to the theory in the specification, how did the Earth's oceans form?
options: Water vapour from volcanoes condensed.
Water vapour from photosynthesis condensed.
The oceans were there when Earth formed.
Water vapour froze and then melted again.
mcqs.explain: Intense volcanic activity released water vapour, which condensed to form the oceans as the Earth cooled.

mcqs.q: Where did the nitrogen in the Earth's atmosphere come from?
options: Algae produced it during photosynthesis.
It was present when the Earth first formed.
It escaped from the oceans as they warmed.
Volcanoes produced it and it built up slowly.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that volcanoes also produced nitrogen, which gradually built up in the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: Which pair of gases may have been present in small proportions in the Earth's early atmosphere?
options: Methane and oxygen
Ammonia and argon
Hydrogen and helium
Methane and ammonia
mcqs.explain: The specification states there may have been small proportions of methane and ammonia.

mcqs.q: When the oceans formed, how was carbon dioxide removed from the atmosphere?
options: It dissolved and carbonates were precipitated.
Sunlight broke it down into carbon and oxygen.
It was used up by animals during respiration.
It reacted with the nitrogen to form nitrates.
mcqs.explain: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated, producing sediments and reducing atmospheric carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: A scientist argues that because Mars and Venus have atmospheres of mainly carbon dioxide, the Earth's early atmosphere was certainly the same. What is the main weakness of this argument?
options: Data sent back by space probes are never reliable.
Other planets may have developed in different ways.
Ideas about the distant past can never be tested.
Carbon dioxide cannot be detected from far away.
mcqs.explain: The comparison supports the theory but does not confirm it; Mars and Venus are different planets with their own histories.

mcqs.q: Which equation represents photosynthesis, as given in the specification?
mcqs.explain: This is the equation given in the specification, and it balances with 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on each side.

mcqs.q: Which process produced the oxygen that is now in the Earth's atmosphere?
options: Respiration by early algae and plants
Volcanic activity on the early Earth
Condensation of the volcanic vapour
Photosynthesis by algae and plants
mcqs.explain: The specification states that algae and plants produced the oxygen now in the atmosphere by photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: About how long ago did algae first produce oxygen?
options: About 4.6 billion years ago
About 200 million years ago
About 2.7 billion years ago
About 1.5 million years ago
mcqs.explain: The specification states that algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago.

mcqs.q: Which sequence matches the way the specification describes the rise of oxygen?
options: Algae made oxygen, then plants evolved, then animals
Plants evolved, then algae made oxygen, then animals
Animals evolved, then algae made oxygen, then plants
Algae made oxygen, then animals evolved, then plants
mcqs.explain: Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago, plants evolved over the next billion years, and the rising percentage of oxygen enabled animals to evolve.

mcqs.q: What effect did the spread of algae and plants have on the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
options: It increased, because photosynthesis makes it.
It decreased, because photosynthesis uses it.
It decreased, because respiration removes it.
It stayed the same, as plants use no gases.
mcqs.explain: Carbon dioxide is a reactant in photosynthesis, so algae and plants decreased the percentage of carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: Apart from photosynthesis, what else decreased the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
options: Carbon became locked in rocks and fossil fuels.
Burning fossil fuels took it out of the air.
Carbon dioxide escaped from Earth into space.
Carbon dioxide was destroyed by the sunlight.
mcqs.explain: Carbon dioxide was also decreased by the formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels that contain carbon.

mcqs.q: How were deposits of limestone formed?
options: From thick deposits of buried plant material
From volcanic ash settling onto the sea bed
From shells and skeletons of marine organisms
From plankton buried in mud on the sea bed
mcqs.explain: Limestone is a sedimentary rock formed from the calcium carbonate shells and skeletons of marine organisms deposited on the sea bed.

mcqs.q: Crude oil and natural gas were formed from the remains of which organisms?
options: Thick deposits of buried plant material
Remains of dinosaurs buried in the rock
Carbonate sediments from the sea water
Plankton buried in mud on the sea floor
mcqs.explain: Crude oil and natural gas formed from plankton, marine organisms buried in mud and altered over millions of years.

mcqs.q: Coal is a sedimentary rock. What was it formed from?
options: Plankton buried in sea-bed mud
Remains of buried land animals
Thick deposits of plant material
Precipitated carbonate sediment
mcqs.explain: Coal formed from thick deposits of plant material that were buried and compressed over millions of years.

mcqs.q: Which pair of changes describes how the Earth's atmosphere changed over most of its history?
options: Carbon dioxide fell and oxygen rose
Carbon dioxide rose and oxygen fell
Both carbon dioxide and oxygen rose
Both carbon dioxide and oxygen fell
mcqs.explain: Carbon dioxide was removed by the oceans, carbonate precipitation, photosynthesis and burial as rocks and fuels, while photosynthesis released oxygen.
